items.title: Bill Holman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 13, 1999
items.q: I did that exact thing. When he was writing for Barnet in 1949 I heard them down in Balboa and they played that... that Shorty had done for Woody. And I went home and tried to write a chart something like that... But yeah, that’s what you do when you’re young... Odd you should mention that, because

ctx.x: Who were your favorites when you were listening to the radio? Let’s say, oh 1940 and you were about 13?

Oh, there were a lot. I always liked Basie’s band, Benny Goodman, I was starting to get into Woody Herman, Charlie Barnet and of course Duke. I didn’t understand Duke though, it was a little deep for me. Basie’s old band, you know with Prez and all those guys, it was right out there. And I never lost a love for that feel, you know that really radical swinging that the Basie band did that at time. It had a small band feel almost.
Curious you used the word “radical.” Why would you say radical swinging?

items.title: 52220_Woody Herman oral history interview
items.q: he was very big influence in that '60s band... he did a big job for us

ctx.x: -- Bill Holman did for the band. Yeah, that's the suite. (unintelligible)

Right, and that actually has some, I think, some significance to the development of the use of the soprano saxophone in a wider way of the last ten years or more, because it predated, say, Wayne Shorter's entry.
